flagged: Vitruvius wrote that Roman harbor concrete becomes "a single stone mass, impregnable to the waves and every day stronger." (false: This is Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 35.166, written in the 1st century AD. Vitruvius wrote earlier (c. 30–22 BC) about volcanic ash, but the quote isn't his. Fix the narration to say "Pliny the Elder" so it matches the caption and on-screen text.)
(Narration) Researchers drilled the cores in 1997. (false: ROMACONS was set up in 2001, and it drilled at Portus Cosanus in June 2003.)

(Narration) The cores were up to about 12 feet (2.25 m) long. (false: Hedged with "up to about". 2.25 m is about 7.4 ft, not 12 ft. The 2.25 m maximum is for the whole 2003 season, which included a core from Santa Liberata.)

(On-screen) ROMACONS took six cores. (false: Verdict: false (in context). Six is the total for the 2003 season, including one core from the Santa Liberata pila, a separate site. The cores taken at Cosa numbered five. Say "five cores at Cosa," or say the six covered two sites.)

(On-screen) The cores were about 1.5 to 7.4 ft (0.48 to 2.25 m) long. (unsupported: Verdict: unsupported (as a figure for Cosa). Hedged with "about". The 0.48–2.25 m range is for all six 2003 cores, including Santa Liberata. I couldn't confirm the range for Cosa's five cores alone. The conversions are fine: 0.48 m ≈ 1.6 ft and 2.25 m ≈ 7.4 ft.)

Nobody has checked whether Cosa's builders used the lime-chunk method; Cosa's concrete hasn't been tested for it. (unsupported: Rated without a full search (search limit reached). I couldn't confirm or rule this out. Leftover lime chunks have been documented in the ROMACONS harbor cores, so "nobody has checked" may overstate it. "We found no published test of Cosa's concrete for this" is safer. No sources confirming.)

(On-screen) No source backs the "lasts 40x longer" figure. (unsupported: Verdict: unsupported (not verified). The search limit stopped me checking this. Calling it a myth is a reasonable editorial call, but I haven't checked it.)

(On-screen) No surviving text gives a full Roman mixing method. (disputed: Rated without a full search (search limit reached). Vitruvius described marine construction with volcanic ash, and one secondary source says he gave a 1:2 lime-to-ash ratio for underwater work. That's not a full recipe, but the line could be read as saying no Roman text covers mixing at all. Suggested wording: "Roman texts give proportions but not a complete method." The Interesting Engineering source is a listicle, so weak support.)

Narration: "In the 9th century" (when the trenches were cut and the work began) (false: The temple dates to the 8th century, credited to Krishna I (r. c. 756–773). One source dates the whole span to the "8–9th centuries," so some later additions may fall in the 9th. But the start of the work, which is what this sentence describes, was in the 8th. Change it to "8th century" to match the caption and on-screen text.)

Narration: They also used picks (unsupported: Only popular websites mention picks. Better sources describe iron chisels, hammers and wooden wedges. Suggested wording: "chisels and hammers." Sources are weak only.)

Narration: "Attributed to Rashtrakuta king Dantidurga" (disputed: The standard attribution is to Krishna I, Dantidurga's successor and uncle. Some scholars (Burgess, Goetz) think work began under Dantidurga, and one source credits both kings. Direct evidence for Dantidurga is lacking. Change to Krishna I, or say "possibly begun under Dantidurga.")

Narration: "The only certainty is the direction they worked" (disputed: Disputed because it overstates. Top-down carving is certain. But the 8th-century date and the Krishna I attribution are also generally treated as solid. What is really debated is how long it took and how many reigns it spanned.)

Caption: The flag pillars are about 50–55 ft (15–17 m) tall (unsupported: Could not confirm the height (searches hit a limit). The pages found mention the pillars but give no measurement. Check this against Wikipedia, the Archaeological Survey of India, or a scholarly source before publishing. No sources found that give a height.)

First comment: The "18 years" figure is a modern estimate, probably based on the length of Krishna I's reign (unsupported: Hedged via "probably." Plausible: one explainer equates "Krishna I's reign" with "roughly 18 years," and popular sites repeat "18 years" without naming any source. But no scholarly source explains where the figure comes from. Keep the hedge. Rests only on weak sources.)

The wreck lies 148 ft (45 m) down (disputed: Hedging is mixed: the narration is unhedged, while the caption and on-screen text are hedged ('about'). 45 m is a common figure, but WHOI reports depths of 40–50 m and Ancient-Greece.org gives about 50–52 m. Suggested wording: 'about 45–50 m down.' The narration should also say 'about.')
Gears were spotted in May 1905 (narration) (false: It was 17 May 1902.)
Spyridon Marinatos spotted the gears (narration) (false: It was archaeologist Valerios Stais.)

Built or made in the 2nd century BC (narration, caption, on-screen twice) (disputed: Estimates of when it was built run from about 205 BC to about 60 BC. Alexander Jones dates the eclipse and games cycles on the dials to 205 BC, which supports the 2nd century. Other estimates are 150–100 BC, about 87 BC, or within a generation before the wreck (about 70–60 BC). Safer wording: '2nd or early 1st century BC.')

The fragments include 37 bronze gears (narration) (false: 30 gears survive: 27 in Fragment A and one each in Fragments B, C and D. The figure of 37 or more appears in less reliable sources as an estimate of the reconstructed total, not a count of surviving gears.)

Others dispute that (narration, on-screen, first comment) (unsupported: The only pushback in the sources found comes from the authors themselves and from press coverage, noting that the measurements may be wrong and that corrosion may have distorted the parts. Either name a critic or reword, e.g. 'the authors caution that corrosion may skew the measurements.' The search quota ran out before a named critic could be sought.)

It came from a 'Greek shipwreck' at the Antikythera Shipwreck, Antikythera, Greece (caption) (disputed: The location is correct. Whose ship it was is described differently: Wikipedia calls it a Roman-era cargo ship from about the second quarter of the 1st century BC, while WHOI calls it a Greek trading ship. Safer wording: 'a shipwreck off Greece.')

"Eight-ton carved pillars" (N) (disputed: Weights are estimates and vary by source. The DAI blog gives about 8–10 metric tons each for the central pair in Enclosure D. Smithsonian quotes Schmidt as saying 7–10 tons for the tallest pillars. Most pillars are smaller, so 'eight-ton pillars' overgeneralizes. Suggested wording: 'pillars weighing up to about 10 tons.')

The oldest enclosures date to about 8500 BC (N) (false: Hedged with 'about'. UNESCO dates the site to 9600–8200 BCE, and the earliest monumental enclosures are from about 9500 BC. 8500 BC falls in the later phase. Should be about 9500 BC. This also contradicts the caption and on-screen text.)

One enclosure's central pillars stand 21 feet (6.4 m) tall (N) (false: The central pair in Enclosure D are about 5.5 m (18 ft). Should be 18 feet (5.5 m). This contradicts the caption and on-screen text.)

"Ian Hodder's team" sorted the bones (N) (false: Should be Klaus Schmidt's team. The count came from Joris Peters (LMU Munich), the archaeozoologist on Klaus Schmidt's excavation. The listed excavators of Göbekli Tepe are Schmidt, Necmi Karul and Lee Clare, not Hodder. Hodder is generally associated with Çatalhöyük, but this could not be confirmed in a search (searches ran out); this does not change the verdict.)

Wild grain traces were found on "thousands of grinding stones" (N) / "over 7,000 grinding tools" (OS) (unsupported: Unsupported as worded. The 2019 PLOS ONE study analysed more than 7,000 grinding and pounding tools. Its evidence for cereals comes from wear marks on handstones and plant microfossils (phytoliths) sampled from grinding surfaces. It doesn't show grain traces on all 7,000 tools. Suggested wording: 'Over 7,000 grinding tools point to large-scale cereal processing.')

Al-Kindi was a Persian scholar. (false: Narration. Al-Kindi (c. 801–873) was an Arab polymath, born in Kufa in Iraq and known as "the philosopher of the Arabs." The Persian scholar was al-Biruni (973–1048), from Khwarazm. Fix: "Arab philosopher al-Kindi," or "Persian scholar al-Biruni.")

Al-Kindi "said the same," meaning he compared the pattern to running water. (unsupported: Narration. Al-Kindi did describe the sword pattern, which he called firind or jawhar. One metallurgy source says this "might be" the first description of the "water" pattern. No source found showing he compared it to running water. A safer line: "al-Kindi described the patterned steel, called firind.")

The last high-quality blades date to about 1650. (false: Narration; hedged with "about." The last blades with the best patterns were made around 1750. Lower-quality patterned blades continued into the early 19th century. Caption and on-screen text already say 1750.)

Vanadium "as little as 400 parts per million." (false: Narration. The correct figure is 40 ppm. One Verhoeven paper puts it at about 0.004% (40 ppm). On-screen text already says 40. The 400 probably comes from the iron Pendray and Verhoeven used, which contained about 0.04% vanadium (400 ppm).)

Al-Biruni compared the patterns to "running water." (unsupported: Caption; also on screen, in quotation marks. One source says al-Biruni "comments on the 'water' pattern." Another reads his "water" as a technical word for one of steel's two parts (dus), not a description of the pattern's look. No source found for the exact words "running water." Remove the quotation marks, or say "al-Biruni wrote about the patterned (firind) steel.")
Camp Century was begun in 1955 (narration). (false: The site was scouted in May 1959. Construction began in June 1959 and was finished by October 1960.)

The base had 26 tunnels. (disputed: The Atomic Heritage Foundation and Polar Journal say 26. Wikipedia, the University of Vermont and BLDGBLOG say 21, and Earth Magazine says "about two dozen." Safer wording: "more than 20 tunnels" or "about two dozen tunnels.")
Iceworm was a plan to hide up to 900 missiles (narration). (false: Hedged with "up to". The plan was for up to 600 missiles. This also contradicts the caption and on-screen text.)
By 1967 the Navy was gone (narration). (false: Camp Century was a US Army base, built by the Army Corps of Engineers, not a Navy one.)

ROMACONS took six cores (on-screen) (false: Must fix. ROMACONS says five cores were taken from Cosa's harbour in 2003: Pier 1, Pier 2 (two cores), Pier 1.5 and Pier 5 (PCO.2003.01–05). A sixth core taken that year came from Santa Liberata, a different site. Change to "five cores.")

Cores were "up to about 7 feet (2.25 m)" (narration) / "about 1.5 to 7.4 feet (0.48 to 2.25 m)" (on-screen) (unsupported: Must fix. Hedged with "up to about" and "about." The core lengths could not be found in any source reached. The conversions themselves are right (0.48 m ≈ 1.57 ft; 2.25 m ≈ 7.38 ft). Remove the figures or check them against the ROMACONS appendix (Brandon/Oleson et al.) or the book Building for Eternity (2014).)

Nobody has checked whether Cosa's builders used hot mixing / Cosa's concrete hasn't been tested for it (narration, caption, on-screen) (unsupported: This claims that something hasn't happened, and it could not be confirmed. Nothing was found showing that Cosa's concrete was studied for hot mixing, but the search limit prevented further checks. Safer: "We found no study testing Cosa's concrete for hot mixing.")

Myth: Roman concrete "lasts 40X longer"; no source backs that figure (on-screen) (unsupported: The search turned up no reliable source for a 40× figure. That fits the script's point, but the fact-checker could not confirm that no such source exists.)

No surviving text gives a full Roman mixing method (on-screen) (disputed: Should soften. Vitruvius (De Architectura, Book 5) gives a marine-concrete ratio of 2 parts volcanic ash to 1 part lime and describes how it was placed. He leaves out details like ash composition, so "full" is a judgement call. Suggested wording: "Vitruvius gives proportions, but no ancient text explains the whole process.")
